prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, transforming the analysis of the gains from trade

statement.case_for: The Melitz (2003) model brought selection of exporters, productivity differences and within-industry reallocation into a tractable general-equilibrium framework. It reorganised both trade theory and the empirical use of firm-level data, and it is now standard graduate material. Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus foreign direct investment is the natural complement. The credit is concentrated and can be stated in a single citation. The work is over twenty years old, so it has been tested across many countries and datasets. It is also a later and distinct advance on the new trade theory recognised in 2008. In my opening I ranked the political-economics candidate (B017) first. After reading colleagues' arguments on attribution and on overlap with the 2024 institutions prize, I now think B044 has the cleaner credit boundary and the lower risk of a topical-overlap objection. My judgement rests on attribution and maturity, not on how many colleagues ranked it highly.
statement.case_against: Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related empirical and quantitative contributions that a two-name prize would not credit. Redding's quantitative extensions are real, though later. Some welfare conclusions depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity and CES preferences, so the quantitative gains from trade are model-dependent. Trade has also had a recent prize (2008), which may weigh on field balance. The strongest reservation is that the foundational idea is largely Melitz's, and Helpman's claim also draws on a broader body of trade-theory work than this ballot defines.

responses.point: Enflo ranks the heterogeneous-firm framework first on transformation, scope and durability, with Melitz as the central contribution and Helpman as the complement. She flags Krugman's 2008 prize and the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum.
responses.response: I agree with the core attribution and the maturity assessment. I qualify the Krugman point. The Melitz framework answers a different question (who gains within industries, and through which firms) and builds on the earlier theory without duplicating it. The omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is a genuine cost. I would handle it through a citation that names the theoretical framework of selection and gains from trade, not the empirical regularities. I do not think a two-name award is wrong on that account, but it should be acknowledged as a limit of the cap.

responses.point: Boppart ranks the labour-demand candidate (B038) first, with Autor, Hanson and Katz. He argues the skill-biased, task-based and China-shock strands are separable and well documented, and notes the overlap with Acemoglu's recent recognition and the arbitrary exclusion of Dorn.
responses.response: I take the empirical credibility of this work seriously and ranked it myself, with Dorn instead of Katz. I am less sure than he is that it is one discovery. It joins a skill-premium literature with a trade-shock literature, and the task framework has contributors outside the list. His own caveats about Acemoglu's overlap and the choice of third name point to the same attribution difficulty. I therefore see a two-strand prize here as harder to cite cleanly than the firm-heterogeneity framework. I keep B038 as an alternative. I do not think it is the weaker case on scientific impact.

responses.point: Hassler ranks political economics second with only Persson and Tabellini, treating Besley's inclusion as a close call, and notes its distinction from the 2024 institutions prize. His first choice is the Kiyotaki-Moore credit-cycle mechanism.
responses.response: I accept that the Besley question is real. My opening included him for the state-capacity strand, but Hassler's two-name version shows that the credit boundary of B017 is less settled than I first treated it. The empirical identification of constitutional effects is also weaker than the theory. That is one reason I moved away from B017 as my first choice, though I still regard it as a field-defining programme and keep it as an alternative. On B037, I agree that Kiyotaki and Moore are a clean two-name attribution. I still ranked it below the trade framework because of the overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises.

uncertainties: Whether Redding, or the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum group not credited on this ballot, should shape the citation or the laureate set.
How much weight the Committee should give to the 2008 trade prize when judging field balance.
How sensitive the quantitative gains-from-trade conclusions are to structural assumptions.
Whether the labour-demand and political-economics candidates have stronger claims on timing than I now credit.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent that would require recusal. Neither Melitz nor Helpman is among my listed co-authors. I have co-authored with Timo Boppart and John Hassler, who are fellow committee members, but neither is credited on the three ballots I discuss. My own work on capital-skill complementarity and inequality is intellectually adjacent to the labour-demand candidate (B038), and my work on the political economy of growth is adjacent to B017. None of the credited names there appears among my documented co-authors.
